newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. believes Iraq still has "missile force".
newsitem.headline: U.N. believes Iraq still has "missile force".

text.p: Chief U.N. arms inspector Rolf Ekeus told the the Security Council on Wednesday he believed Iraq still had "a significant number of operational missiles which could constitute a complete missile force."
While there was a "theoretical possibility" Iraq had destroyed those missiles secretly, it had not displayed the scrapped rockets, he told reporters.

Under resolutions after the 1991 Gulf War calling for the destruction of Iraq's nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile potential, Baghdad is barred from possessing rockets with a range greater than 150 km, or 93 miles.

Ekeus briefed the council on his latest visit to Baghdad, from Dec. 8 to 11, and said he had again been unable to secure permission to remove for analysis in the United States SCUD missile engines and other components which Iraq destroyed and buried without U.N. supervision shortly after the war.
Iraq had first prevented U.N. weapons inspectors in November from taking the excavated missile parts out of the country to try to obtain a definitive accounting of any remaining stocks.

Ekeus said he told the Security Council: "We believe that Iraq is still holding a significant number of operational missiles which could constitute a complete missile force, including all support equipment, rocket fuel, launchers and everything."
There was a "theoretical possibility that Iraq has destroyed these missiles secretly...But then I took it that Iraq should show us the destroyed missiles. So that is a concern we have," he added.
A complete accounting of all Iraq's weapons of mass destruction is a key requirement for the lifting of sanctions imposed by the Security Council after Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Ekeus declined to say how many missiles Iraq might still have, except to say there were "enough to make up a missile force of significance."

He has previously said between six and 16 missiles remained unaccounted for, but now seemed to be suggesting a larger number. The shortest range of any of the missing SCUDs was about 190 miles (300 km), he said.

During 15 hours of detailed, highly technical meetings with Iraqi deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz and other officials, "it appeared that the technical process only widened, in a sense, the gap in assessments," he said.

Ekeus said Iraq was shown documents proving the export to Iraq by a certain country -- presumably the then-Soviet Union -- of specific missiles, each with an identifying number, as well as data from inside Iraq proving the receipt of the missiles.
"We haven't found any of these specifically numbered and identified missiles in Iraq," he said.
Ekeus said Aziz undertook to investigate and "try to find responses to the concerns and problems raised." Another meeting would be held in February.
Security Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy said later several members expressed concern at Ekeus's report.

The council expressed the hope that the "new atmosphere" after the recent start of an "oil-for-food scheme" permitting Iraq to sell limited quantities of oil would enable U.N. weapons inspectors to continue their work "with the precision and accuracy which the case needs," Fulci added.
